text: In moderation, yes. A part-time job teaches responsibility, time management and teamwork, which you can't really learn from textbooks. It also gives students a bit of financial independence. The risk is when they work so many hours that their grades suffer. I think around ten to fifteen hours a week is manageable, and ideally the job should relate in some way to what they're studying.

text: The classic problem is the catch-22: employers want experience, but you can't get experience without a job. On top of that, there's often a lot of competition for entry-level positions. I think internships and apprenticeship schemes can bridge that gap, because they let young people build skills while earning a little. Companies also benefit, as they can train potential employees according to their own standards.

tips.en: A paradox explains the problem briefly and clearly.

tips.ru: Парадокс объясняет проблему кратко и ясно.
tips.example: employers want experience, but you can't get experience without a job

text: Generally speaking, yes, up to a point. If the salary can't cover your basic needs, then constant financial worry will outweigh any enjoyment. But once you have a comfortable income, extra money doesn't add much to happiness, whereas meaningful work does. Personally, I'd accept a slightly lower salary for a job where I feel valued and can learn new things.

text: I think routine tasks, such as data entry or basic customer service, will be automated first. That will probably create new roles, like AI trainers or ethics specialists, but it may take time for workers to adapt. Schools could help by focusing less on memorising facts and more on critical thinking and creativity, since those are the skills machines find hardest to copy.
